title: China’s Quiet Quest to Dominate Latin America
gist: China has abandoned Belt and Road megaprojects in Latin America for cheap, low-visibility subnational deals — surveillance cameras, police gear, electric buses, power distributors, lithium stakes — that individually escape statistical capture and collectively create hard-to-reverse dependence. Sovereign lending fell from roughly $25 billion in 2010 to about $1.3 billion a year while commercial Chinese investment held near $8.5 billion in 2024, and U.S. policy remains aimed at the old megaproject playbook.

themes.theme: The pivot from megaprojects to 'small but beautiful'

insights.claim: China shifted away from Latin American megaprojects in the early 2020s because big projects cost too much amid domestic economic strain and drew disproportionate geopolitical backlash.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Tracking Chinese influence by megaproject headlines now systematically understates it; the exposure has moved to municipal procurement.
insights.locator: But starting in the early 2020s, China changed course

insights.claim: The core insight is that China is pioneering a statecraft model built on quiet subnational capture rather than large visible assets, deliberately bypassing high-visibility sectors like ports and 5G where it faces pushback.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for reading Chinese influence anywhere in the global South: follow procurement contracts and maintenance agreements, not FDI headlines.
insights.quote: Beijing, in other words, is pioneering a kind of statecraft that privileges quiet, subnational capture over big, flashy projects.
insights.locator: These endeavors are not unique to Latin America

insights.claim: China's strategy in Latin America has no single point of failure by design, spreading across municipal, provincial, and national relationships including nearly 180 sister-city agreements with 17 Latin American countries.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: There is no chokepoint for U.S. countermeasures to target, which makes the influence far more durable than port or telecom concentration.
insights.quote: nearly 180 sister-city agreements with 17 Latin American countries
insights.locator: BOTTOM UP

insights.claim: Beijing itself uses the 'small but beautiful' label narrowly, reserving it in its 2025 Latin America white paper for small poverty-reduction projects, so the phrase understates the strategy it actually describes.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Official Chinese terminology should not be taken as the boundary of the practice it names.
insights.locator: Beijing itself applies this label narrowly

themes.theme: Money moved from sovereign loans to commercial acquisitions

insights.claim: Traditional Belt and Road lending to Latin America collapsed from nearly $25 billion in 2010 to an average of $1.3 billion a year, a roughly 95 percent decline in the headline metric most analysts track.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The most-cited China-in-LatAm indicator has cratered while actual engagement held up — a classic measurement trap for macro analysts.
insights.quote: Traditional Belt and Road loans to the region have faded from nearly $25 billion in 2010 to an average of $1.3 billion a year.
insights.locator: To see how important this model has become

insights.claim: Firm-level tracking shows Chinese companies still invested $8.5 billion in Latin America in 2024, down only about a tenth year over year, and the author judges that figure to be an undercount.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Chinese capital deployment in the region is roughly flat, not retreating; the composition changed, not the volume.
insights.quote: Chinese companies still invested $8.5 billion in Latin America in 2024, down just a tenth from the year before—and that figure is likely an undercount.
insights.locator: But judging by estimates that track deals firm by firm

insights.claim: Chinese money now enters through commercial transactions and acquisitions of existing assets such as power distributors and mines, rather than sovereign loans funding new construction.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Screen for Chinese acquirers in Latin American utility and mining M&A, where control transfers quietly without a state-loan signature.
insights.locator: The difference is that this money now flows

insights.claim: Equipment sales, training programs, donations, and maintenance contracts are booked as procurement rather than investment, so they escape investment statistics entirely and often surface only when a local journalist finds the contract.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The data gap is structural, not accidental — any model of Chinese exposure built on FDI series is missing the fastest-growing channel.
insights.locator: Because these deals are for items that investment statistics

insights.claim: Chinese firms operate every power distributor serving Lima and control commuter rail on all three of Buenos Aires's main electric lines, giving Beijing operational positions in two of the region's largest metros.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Urban electricity and rail are hard-to-substitute utilities; these are concentrated single-city dependencies already in place.
insights.locator: They operate every power distributor serving

insights.claim: In Argentina's lithium-rich Jujuy Province, a geological-agency research exchange escalated into a formal state partnership surveying the salt flats, after which a Chinese company took a majority stake in a local lithium project.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: A template for resource capture: technical cooperation first, state agreement second, majority equity third — watch early-stage research MOUs as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: For example, in Argentina’s lithium-rich Jujuy Province

themes.theme: Security and surveillance as the entry vector

insights.claim: Latin America's homicide rate of roughly 20 per 100,000 — three times the global average — creates persistent political demand for visible security spending that China supplies more cheaply than anyone else.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The demand driver is structural and won't fade, so Chinese security vendors have a durable pipeline regardless of U.S. pressure.
insights.quote: the homicide rate is around 20 per 100,000—three times the global average
insights.locator: Safety is a major political issue in Latin America

insights.claim: The engagement escalates from rudimentary donated goods — anti-riot gear and armored vehicles for Bolivia's armed forces, motorcycles for Caribbean police — to sophisticated integrated systems.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Small donations are the leading indicator of a lock-in sequence, not a trivial gesture.
insights.locator: Recipient countries often start by acquiring rudimentary provisions

insights.claim: Rio de Janeiro's governor signed deals with Hikvision and Dahua in April 2025 for more than 27,000 body and vehicle cameras, and Ciudad Juárez bought 1,000 facial-recognition cameras from the same two vendors despite both being on the FCC's prohibited list.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: U.S. entity-listing has no extraterritorial bite on Latin American municipal buyers — sanctioned vendors keep winning contracts next door to El Paso.
insights.quote: signed deals with the Chinese surveillance technology companies Hikvision and Dahua for more than 27,000 body and vehicle cameras
insights.locator: In April 2025, for example

insights.claim: By 2018, 62 percent of Argentina's surveillance equipment imports came from China versus five percent from the United States, and at least 35 Latin American cities now run Chinese surveillance systems.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: A greater-than-12-to-1 import share gap means the U.S. is not a marginal competitor in this category — it is absent.
insights.quote: By 2018, 62 percent of Argentina’s surveillance equipment imports came from China, compared with just five percent from the United States. Today, at least 35 Latin American cities use Chinese surveillance systems.
insights.locator: By 2018, 62 percent of Argentina’s surveillance

insights.claim: Ecuador's ECU-911 emergency system was financed by a $240 million China Development Bank loan secured not by sovereign collateral but by a PetroEcuador contract to ship 72,000 barrels a day to PetroChina over the system's operating life.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Oil-collateralized security infrastructure ties a country's crude output to a surveillance contract — an unusual, under-modeled form of sovereign encumbrance.
insights.quote: A $240 million China Development Bank loan financed the system, secured not by sovereign collateral but by an oil sales contract committing PetroEcuador, Ecuador’s state oil company, to ship 72,000 barrels a day to PetroChina over the system’s operating life.
insights.locator: Consider, for example, the development of ECU-911

insights.claim: China bundles police training with hardware, sending Argentine, Brazilian, Cuban, and Panamanian delegations to the China Criminal Investigation Police University in Shenyang and signing a September 2024 narcotics, cybercrime, and terrorism training agreement with Nicaragua's police.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The U.S. still trains more Latin American police, but its courses are unbundled — training without hardware does not create switching costs.
insights.locator: Finally, China has been training Latin America’s law enforcement

insights.claim: Chinese camera designs are largely proprietary and often impossible to service without continued Chinese assistance, so routine equipment failure forces cities back to Chinese vendors rather than opening a competitive replacement bid.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Maintenance, not the initial sale, is where the recurring dependency and the pricing power sit.
insights.quote: China, for example, builds the world’s most economical and widely adopted surveillance systems.
insights.locator: DURABLE BY DESIGN

insights.claim: A 2020 study could not identify a single government that adopted a Chinese surveillance and policing platform and then fully removed it; governments restricted specific features instead of ripping systems out.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Empirically zero exit rate — treat any Chinese platform adoption as effectively permanent when modeling country risk.
insights.quote: There is a reason why a 2020 study was unable to locate a single government that adopted a Chinese surveillance and policing platform and then completely got rid of it.
insights.locator: Replacing them is extremely expensive

insights.claim: The dependency converts into a coercion tool: if a state opposes Beijing's interests, China can withhold spare parts, software updates, and technicians, turning a commercial contract into political leverage.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Latin American voting behavior in multilateral fora may increasingly track infrastructure dependency rather than stated alignment.
insights.locator: As a result, many Latin American countries are highly vulnerable

insights.claim: ECU-911 demonstrates that lock-in persists even when the system fails: Ecuadorian homicides rose from about 1,000 in 2016 to over 4,800 in 2022, roughly 1,100 of 6,500 cameras were offline by 2022, and the system barely functions today — yet replacement remains prohibitively costly.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Product performance is not the binding constraint on dependency — switching cost is, which means poor Chinese execution does not self-correct the exposure.
insights.quote: homicides in Ecuador rose from about 1,000 in 2016 to over 4,800 in 2022
insights.locator: ECU-911 never measurably reduced crime

insights.claim: Telecom precedent confirms the lock-in: Huawei built and still services the 4G networks of three of Brazil's four major carriers, which made it impossible for Jair Bolsonaro to ban the company from 5G despite trying.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Even an ideologically hostile head of state could not reverse embedded Chinese infrastructure — political will is not sufficient to unwind these positions.
insights.quote: The 4G networks of three of Brazil’s four major carriers, for example, were built by and are still serviced by Huawei, which made it impossible for former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro to ban the company from 5G networks, despite his best efforts.
insights.locator: The same lock-in has already played out in telecommunications

insights.claim: Chinese firms, backed by generous home-government subsidies, drive domestic competitors out of business in the markets where they sell, eliminating local alternatives before dependency becomes politically salient.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Subsidy-driven predatory pricing destroys the substitute supply base, so the lock-in is manufactured upstream of the contract.
insights.locator: In the countries where it sells them

insights.claim: Honduras broke relations with Taiwan in March 2023, signed 17 cooperation agreements with China three months later including one on smart cities, endorsed China's Global Security Initiative, and within a year awarded an uncompetitive contract for a Chinese video-management system and installed 3,500 Huawei cameras.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Diplomatic derecognition of Taiwan now front-runs procurement wins — the sequence is a measurable, repeatable pattern to watch in remaining Taiwan-recognizing states.
insights.locator: In March 2023, for instance, Honduras broke off

insights.claim: Chinese-backed projects can trigger domestic repression: when indigenous groups blockaded Argentina's salt flats over lithium projects, Jujuy's governor fast-tracked a constitutional reform banning road blockades and provincial police allegedly assaulted and illegally detained protesters.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Social-license and ESG risk in Latin American lithium is materially higher where Chinese capital is the counterparty, because local governments have shown they will legislate around opposition.

themes.theme: Global replication and the U.S. policy lag

insights.claim: China's Ministry of Public Security has signed policing or security agreements with some 74 countries covering more than 200 deals, and has verifiably trained more than 12,000 foreign officers since 2000.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The model is global, not regional — sizing the Chinese security-export market off Latin America alone undercounts it by an order of magnitude.
insights.quote: China’s Ministry of Public Security has signed policing or security agreements with some 74 countries—featuring more than 200 deals in all. It has verifiably trained more than 12,000 foreign officers since 2000.
insights.locator: Little wonder, then, that China runs the same model

insights.claim: The same playbook runs in Pakistan, where the Punjab Safe Cities Authority installed Huawei command centers and 10,000 cameras on an $84.7 million contract, and in Kenya, whose surveillance system runs on Chinese technology.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Roughly $8,500 per camera-node deployment gives a rough unit economics benchmark for pricing the global safe-city market.
insights.quote: the Punjab Safe Cities Authority installed Huawei-built command centers and 10,000 surveillance cameras on an $84.7 million contract
insights.locator: In the Pakistani city of Lahore

insights.claim: China even made subnational inroads inside the United States by selling port cranes to local authorities and operators for years before the federal government moved to stop it.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: The subnational-capture vulnerability is not a developing-world phenomenon; U.S. local procurement is exposed by the same mechanism.
insights.locator: Even in the United States, China made subnational inroads

insights.claim: Chinese doctrine follows practice rather than preceding it: the 2008 and 2016 Latin America policy papers treated regional security as a sidebar, while the December 2025 paper made security cooperation central only after the contracts were already functioning.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Reading Chinese white papers as forward guidance is backward — they ratify what already happened, so on-the-ground contracts lead policy by years.
insights.quote: In Chinese statecraft, doctrine does not always precede action.
insights.locator: In Chinese statecraft, doctrine does not always precede

insights.claim: U.S. policy remains aimed at the old playbook of ports, 5G, and space infrastructure rather than municipal procurement offices and police academies, and the author argues Washington must instead supply durable, effective solutions to those actors' actual problems.
insights.speaker: Natalia Cote-Muñoz
insights.so_what: Absent a U.S. offering at competitive price and speed, condemnation and visa revocations will not change procurement outcomes — China stays the default supplier.
insights.locator: Because China’s doctrine ratified practice
